subject: Using Likert-scale in an ideal point model? matrix?

messages.author: f4c2e63aec3c6db2
messages.subject: Using Likert-scale in an ideal point model? matrix?
parts:
Hi,

Is there a recommended transformation or model adjustment when one wants
to use Likert values (1-5) in an ideal point model? I believe one of
Andrew's post mentions turning responses into z-scores.

For example, I currently have recoded the Likert values to be binary
(above/below mean for sample), which I think is a bad idea for some of
the items.

The guts of the model follow the recommendations in ARM (14.3).

transformed parameters {
for (i in 1:N) {
if (person[i] == person_index_constrain_positive) {
y_hat[i] <- gamma[question[i]] * (fabs(alpha[person[i]]) - beta[question[i]]);
} else {
y_hat[i] <- gamma[question[i]] * (alpha[person[i]] - beta[question[i]]);
}
}
}
model {
y ~ bernoulli_logit(y_hat);
}

Thanks,

Allen

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using Likert-scale in an ideal point model? matrix?
parts:
This isn't answering your question, but I'd recommend replacing
fabs() with exp() to avoid the multimodality inherent in fabs().

- Bob

messages.author: 6b3b475e6af83898
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using Likert-scale in an ideal point model? matrix?
parts:
Not sure if this helps, but do note the existence of the ordered and positive_ordered data types, and the ordered_logistic distribution, which you might use instead of the bernoulli_logit. You could use ordered (or positive_ordered) to hold k-1 cutpoints (for a Likert scale with k options), then use ordered_logistic to estimate the cutpoints.

That generates a graded response model, if you estimate the cutpoints separately for each item. If you have only one set of cutpoints, it would be a rating scale model. There’s been a fair bit of list discussion about how to code a GRM lately, which should get you started.

OTOH, if the Likert scale has an obvious division and you don’t care about the finer details (e.g., Strongly Agree, Agree, Don’t know, Disagree, Strongly Disagree; it only matters if someone agrees at all), then it could make sense to collapse the categories and do the simpler bernoulli_logit (but I wouldn’t just cut arbitrarily at the sample average). Doing that does throw out information which might be meaningful in assessing item difficulty or a person’s ability (if, for instance, a more able person is more likely to select the “strongly” version). If the options aren’t inherently ordered (multiple choice, but not Likert) you could either score it and analyze right/wrong using bernoulli_logit, or code it as a GPCM. I haven’t seen that discussed on the list, but should work if you use a vector instead of ordered, and use categorical_logit instead of bernoulli_logit.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using Likert-scale in an ideal point model? matrix?
parts:
No, with

value <- exp(value_raw);

If you put it in an if-else, you get a non-differentiable
point at zero rather than nice smooth behavior.

But if you want cutpoints for ordinal logit, then there are
ordered and positive ordered vector types that do it for you.

- Bob
